raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Overview

In pull mode, a READ on a wedged connection stays in `PROC` and never fails, and the connection is never taken out of use, since that only happens on an error or when the engine has no reads in flight. So every later request prefilled on that engine reads over the same connection, hangs, and pins its blocks.

This marks the engine invalid once one of its READs has been in flight for `stalled_read_timeout` (480 s by default), the same way it is already handled when its NIXL metadata is lost: new reads to that engine go straight to `kv_load_failure_policy`, and once the stalled READs finish, the engine is released and re-handshaked.

Partially addresses #59971. No other open PR addresses this.

## Claims

- After the deadline, new requests whose KV is on the stalled engine don't read from it and don't pin blocks. Other engines are unaffected.
- If the stalled READs finish, the engine is released and re-handshaked on the next request.
- Adds `stalled_read_timeout` (default 480 s, set to 0 to disable). Push mode is unchanged.

## Validation

`pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py -k "TestPeerReplacement or stalled_read"`: 30 passed, including two new cases.

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Blocks pinned at the end | 470 (78.5%) | 55 (9.2%) |
| READs posted to `bad` | 5 | 1 |
| Requests from `bad` | all 5 hang until abort | 1 hangs, 4 fail right away |
| Next request from `bad` after the READs finish | reuses the connection and hangs | re-handshakes and completes |

The 55 blocks and the one hanging request are the first read from `bad`, posted before the deadline. The four later requests from `bad` are rejected and pin nothing. Those 55 blocks are freed once that READ finishes (see below for why not earlier).

## Details

Flow on `main` (D = decode, E = prefill engine with one wedged connection):

1. Request A is prefilled on E. D starts reading its KV, and one READ stays in `PROC`.
2. A never finishes receiving, so its blocks stay pinned, even after the client aborts.
3. E always has a READ in flight, so it is never evicted or invalidated.
4. Request B from E reads over the same connection. Back to 2.

With this PR, D records a deadline when it starts a request's READs. Past it, E is marked invalid, so B is rejected at step 4 before any READ is posted.

The engine is only marked invalid, not disconnected right away. Disconnecting removes E's remote metadata, and NIXL then reports the stalled READ as failed even though the transfer underneath may still be writing into A's blocks. Freeing those blocks at that point would let the late write corrupt whichever request gets them next. So the existing cleanup waits for in-flight READs to actually finish before it releases an invalid engine, and this PR keeps that.

do you have any idea what causes a request to get stuck in PROC? I would like to make sure we understand this so we can decide how to handle it in vLLM

I found a way to get a READ stuck in PROC like this and wrote it up on #59971 with a script: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59971#issuecomment-6149474364. In that repro, the prefill side fails to create the QP for an incoming connection, UCX drops it without telling the decode side, and the decode ep waits in wireup forever.

The decode side gets no error at all there, so vLLM needs a deadline regardless of what triggers it. Without this PR, one wedged connection keeps pinning blocks for every request sent to that engine. With it, new requests from that engine are rejected once the deadline passes instead of pinning blocks. Bringing the engine back takes a fresh connection, and the repro shows one does recover it.

I pushed the review changes in 0058f01a03. If that sounds right to you, I can follow up with re-handshaking the engine after the deadline.

`decoder_kv_blocks_ttl` controls how long D-side blocks are retained in bidirectional mode, which is meant for tuning based on multi-turn request arrival rate.
Reusing it for detecting stalled READs may cause problems, for eg. lowering it to free D blocks sooner for bi-directional mode will start marking healthy peers invalid on long READS and raising it for long gaps between multi-turns delay the stall detection.

Please add a dedicated config for READ stall detection.

Agreed it shouldn't wait forever, but I don't think we can fail it safely yet. Releasing a handle that's still PROC doesn't stop the READ: NIXL calls ucp_request_cancel, which only cancels tag receives, so the GET can still complete later. If the scheduler has freed or recomputed those blocks by then, the late write lands in another request's KV.

It becomes safe once the QPs are gone, i.e. once remove_remote_agent force-closes the endpoints (nixl#2365, merged but not released). So I'd keep this PR to rejecting new reads and do the abort after the NIXL bump. Does that work for you?

@@ -132,6 +132,11 @@ python tests/v1/kv_connector/nixl_integration/toy_proxy_server.py \
     - In bidirectional mode, the decoder caches KV blocks for multi-turn conversations. This TTL controls how long those blocks are held before being released. Unlike the prefiller lease, this TTL is not renewed via heartbeats.
     - Example: `--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector_extra_config": {"decoder_kv_blocks_ttl": 600}}'`
 
+- `stalled_read_timeout` (via `kv_connector_extra_config`): Timeout (in seconds) for a KV read in pull mode. (Optional)
+    - Default: 480. Set to 0 to disable.
+    - A read still in flight after this long means the connection to that remote engine is stuck. New requests whose KV is on that engine follow `kv_load_failure_policy` instead of waiting on it.
+    - Example: `--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector_extra_config": {"stalled_read_timeout": 300}}'`
+
 ## Bidirectional KV Transfer (Multi-turn)
 
 In standard disaggregated prefilling, KV cache flows in one direction: Prefill (P) computes the KV cache and Decode (D) reads from P. For multi-turn conversations this is wasteful — D already holds the KV cache corresponding to the generated tokens from prior turns, yet P must recompute it from scratch on every new turn. Bidirectional KV transfer lets P **pull** existing KV blocks from D via RDMA before computing only the new tokens, significantly reducing Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) for long-prefill such as **multi-turn heavy scenarios**.

Reusing it for detecting stalled READs may cause problems, for eg. lowering it to free D blocks sooner for bi-directional mode will start marking healthy peers invalid on long READS and raising it for long gaps between multi-turns delay the stall detection.

Please add a dedicated config for READ stall detection.

inline_comments.body:
Agreed it shouldn't wait forever, but I don't think we can fail it safely yet. Releasing a handle that's still PROC doesn't stop the READ: NIXL calls ucp_request_cancel, which only cancels tag receives, so the GET can still complete later. If the scheduler has freed or recomputed those blocks by then, the late write lands in another request's KV.

It becomes safe once the QPs are gone, i.e. once remove_remote_agent force-closes the endpoints (nixl#2365, merged but not released). So I'd keep this PR to rejecting new reads and do the abort after the NIXL bump. Does that work for you?

do you have any idea what causes a request to get stuck in PROC? I would like to make sure we understand this so we can decide how to handle it in vLLM

I found a way to get a READ stuck in PROC like this and wrote it up on #59971 with a script: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59971#issuecomment-6149474364. In that repro, the prefill side fails to create the QP for an incoming connection, UCX drops it without telling the decode side, and the decode ep waits in wireup forever.

The decode side gets no error at all there, so vLLM needs a deadline regardless of what triggers it. Without this PR, one wedged connection keeps pinning blocks for every request sent to that engine. With it, new requests from that engine are rejected once the deadline passes instead of pinning blocks. Bringing the engine back takes a fresh connection, and the repro shows one does recover it.

I pushed the review changes in 0058f01a03. If that sounds right to you, I can follow up with re-handshaking the engine after the deadline.
